The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

Let \(N=2100\). For a prime \(p\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\).

When Mark replaces \(a,b\) by \(\gcd(a,b)\) and \(\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)\), then for each prime \(p\) the two \(p\)-exponents are replaced by their minimum and maximum. Thus, for each prime \(p\), the multiset of \(p\)-exponents on the board is invariant.

At the stopping moment, no pair of numbers can be incomparable by divisibility; otherwise replacing them by their gcd and lcm would change the board. Hence the final board is a divisibility chain. Listing the final numbers as

\[
c_1\le c_2\le \cdots \le c_{2100},
\]

we have \(c_i\mid c_j\) whenever \(i<j\). Therefore, for each prime \(p\), the sequence

\[
v_p(c_1),v_p(c_2),\dots,v_p(c_{2100})
\]

is nondecreasing. Since the multiset of these exponents is the original multiset

\[
\{v_p(1),v_p(2),\dots,v_p(2100)\},
\]

we must have

\[
v_p(c_i)=\text{the }i\text{-th smallest value among }v_p(1),\dots,v_p(2100).
\]

So the final board is forced.

We need the \(2026\)-th smallest final number. Since there are \(2100\) numbers, the \(2026\)-th smallest is the

\[
2100-2026+1=75
\]

th largest.

For a fixed prime \(p\), the number of integers \(n\le 2100\) with \(v_p(n)\ge t\) is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor.
\]

The \(75\)-th largest \(p\)-exponent is therefore the largest \(t\) such that

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor\ge 75.
\]

Since

\[
\frac{2100}{75}=28,
\]

this is equivalent to

\[
p^t\le 28.
\]

Now list the possibilities:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p & \max\{t: p^t\le 28\} \\ \hline
2 & 4 \\
3 & 3 \\
5 & 2 \\
7,11,13,17,19,23 & 1 \\
p\ge 29 & 0
\end{array}
\]

Thus the \(2026\)-th smallest final number is

\[
2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Its number of positive divisors is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 64
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
